newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal minority govt safe from budget crisis.
newsitem.headline: Portugal minority govt safe from budget crisis.

text.p: Portugal's main opposition group says it will not let the minority Socialist government fall in a vote on the 1997 budget even if the pro-European party dislikes parts of the plan to secure membership of the EMU.

Social Democrat (PSD) party leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa told Reuters his party opposed fresh elections before 1998 at the earliest. It would abstain in parliament if the government turned the budget into a confidence vote, he said.
"If we see that there could be a political crisis over the rejection of the budget then we will abstain. If we abstain, this means the budget passes," he said in an interview on Monday night.

The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, which toppled the PSD from power in elections exactly one year ago, must present its budget plan to parliament before October 15. A vote is expected in November.

The ruling party is four seats short of an absolute majority in the 230-seat chamber, elected for four years. It pushed its 1996 budget through with the backing of the small, right-wing Popular Party after the PSD and the Communists voted against.

Rebelo de Sousa, whose conservative party ruled for 17 years until the 1995 elections, said the PSD was as committed as the government to seeing Portugal in the first wave of European Union countries to wed their economies in Economic and Monetary Union in January 1999.
"The PSD was the first party to say that...monetary union was an absolute national priority," he said.
But the opposition leader said that while agreeing with the Socialists on EMU, it differed with the ruling party over the route being taken to get there.
He said that the PSD wanted to see more decisive cuts in state spending, along with moves to reform the country's social welfare system to restrict beneficiaries to the really poor.
Neverthless, he said the only circumstances under which the PSD would vote against the budget plan would be if the government gave a prior undertaking not to resign if defeated.
But he said that the indications were that the government would treat the budget as an all-or-nothing confrontation.
He denied that reluctance to force early elections had anything to do with his party's poor showing in the opinion polls which continue to give a healthy lead to the Socialists.
A national election campaign next year could torpedo Portugal's chances of qualifying for the single currency, he said.
Entry to EMU demands that aspiring members have a budget deficit of no more than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- the measure of economic output -- next year.

With inflation easing and the EU likely to be flexible on debt levels -- two other requirements -- the budget deficit could be the key test for Portugal. The gap between spending and government income is forecast at around four percent in 1996.

The government says the targets can be achieved without huge sacrifices. It rejected a leaked International Monetary Fund (IMF) report on Tuesday which called for wage freezes and public sector lay-offs.

Rebelo de Sousa said that he, too, was confident that Portugal could meet the terms of the single currency and dismissed any suggestion of a special EMU tax along the lines of that recently announced by Italy.

He said that such a tax could weaken support for the European Union at a time when the country -- until now one of the main destinations of EU development funds -- was already going to start reaping fewer direct benefits from membership.
